strengths: Addresses important gap in evaluating cultural representation in T2I models through social activities rather than objects, with clear motivation
Substantial benchmark contribution (576 prompts, 16 countries, 19,000+ images) with systematic coverage of Global North and South
Novel AHEaD evaluation framework with interpretable descriptor-based metrics that demonstrate 7% better correlation with human judgments than VLM-based approaches
Rigorous human evaluation with proper quality controls (domain expertise verification, attention checks, consistency testing) confirming metric validity
Clear finding of systematic Global North bias across all tested T2I models (4-8% performance gaps) with detailed dimensional analysis
Addresses genuine limitation of existing metrics: showing that image-text alignment correlates positively with exaggeration while humans expect negative correlation
Comprehensive reproducibility support including detailed methodology, prompts in appendix, ablation studies, and threshold calibration explanation
weaknesses: Framework relies on LLM-generated descriptors which inherit Western-centric biases; while descriptor accuracy validated at 90.27% average, impact on final metrics across regions not analyzed
Human evaluation limited to 7 of 16 countries (44%) and 3 of 6 models (50%) with moderate human-human agreement (0.42-0.46), limiting confidence in generalization claims
Exaggeration metric design underspecified: selection of exaggeration candidates Sr is unclear, and metric fundamentally depends on noisy real image baselines subject to CLIPScore filtering bias
Threshold calibration (τ=0.52, 75th percentile) appears arbitrary; calibration on biased real images limits robustness; different thresholds may systematically favor different regions
Hallucination metric may incorrectly penalize valid cultural alternatives not in LLM-generated descriptors; limited validation that metric aligns with human hallucination understanding
Activity selection sourced from English-heavy CulturalAtlas and Wikipedia without analysis of representativeness across Global South countries
Real image collection methodology appears limited (20 candidates per prompt → 5 selected via CLIPScore), insufficient to capture activity variation across 16 countries
Statistical rigor lacking: no confidence intervals, significance tests, or p-values reported; 4-8% GN-GS gap claimed important without formal significance testing
Inconsistent metric behavior across perspectives: Figure 7 shows ALIGN/EXAG correlate differently with human scores than with model metrics, questioning what combined FAITH metric measures
Missing comparisons with concurrent work (CuRe, Nayak et al. 2025) beyond citations; limited exploration of sensitivity to proposer LLM choice (only GPT-4o and Gemini tested)

strengths: Important shift from object-centric to activity-centric cultural evaluation with well-motivated justification
Substantial benchmark with 576 prompts across 16 countries, 19,000+ images, and human evaluation with quality controls
Novel metrics distinguishing hallucination from exaggeration, showing clear conceptual advances over image-text alignment
Systematic demonstration that all six T2I models show 4-8% performance gaps favoring Global North countries
AHEaD metrics achieve 0.38 correlation with human judgment vs ~0.05 for existing baselines
Multi-level interpretability (image sets, individual images, specific elements) rather than opaque single scores
weaknesses: Critical circular reasoning: uses LLM-generated descriptors to evaluate LLM/VLM bias in T2I models; LLM descriptor accuracy varies by country (85.21% Iran vs 91.68% Brazil), potentially biasing results for Global South
Human evaluation limited to 7 of 16 countries (189 forms) with modest inter-rater agreement (0.30-0.46); generalization of correlation claims is questionable
Two of four proposed metrics (Descriptor Diversity and Semantic Diversity) completely lack human validation; paper acknowledges but offers no alternative
Exaggeration metric performance is weak (0.26 correlation with human judgment) with inconsistent Regional performance (0.12 GN vs 0.30 GS)
Real images filtered using CLIPScore—a metric the paper criticizes for cultural bias—introducing potential systematic bias into ground truth
Best metric achieves only 0.38 correlation vs. human-human agreement of 0.42; improvements are often 0.01-0.02 with no significance testing
Global North bias finding lacks mechanistic explanation: unclear whether bias stems from T2I models, training data, or LLM descriptor generation bias itself
Asymmetric model evaluation: only 1 image per proprietary model vs 10 per public model makes diversity metrics unvalidated for newer models
Design choices appear arbitrary (threshold τ at Q3, simple arithmetic mean for faithfulness, temperature settings) with minimal justification or sensitivity analysis
Missing actionable insights: paper identifies bias but provides limited guidance on how practitioners should use results to improve models

strengths: Addresses important, understudied problem: evaluating cultural representation in T2I models through social activities rather than objects
Substantial benchmark resource: 576 prompts across 16 countries, 9 activity categories, 19,000+ images, with scalable systematic approach using CulturalAtlas and Wikipedia
Novel evaluation framework: AHEaD metrics using external visual descriptors instead of biased VLMs, providing interpretable feedback across multiple cultural dimensions
Strong empirical validation: 0.38 Spearman correlation with human judgment vs. 0.05-0.22 for existing methods; 7% improvement over baselines
Clear demonstration of systematic bias: 4-8% Global North bias across all models, with insightful finding that models fail worst on culturally-grounded activities
Rigorous human evaluation: domain expertise constraints, 216 evaluation forms, multiple QC measures (attention checks, consistency validation, free-text rationales)
Comprehensive analysis: per-country performance, activity-level breakdown, metric correlations, and ablations; proposer-refiner approach improves descriptor quality
Well-written and well-motivated: clear presentation with effective use of examples and figures; good problem framing using film analogy
weaknesses: Fundamental LLM bias dependency: relies on LLM-generated descriptors as ground truth while criticizing VLM bias; validation covers only 7/16 countries with no analysis of where descriptor quality degrades for Global South

Exaggeration metric methodology unclear: selection of 'exaggeration candidates Sr' is vague; using LLM-identified stereotypes to detect bias against stereotypes is conceptually problematic; Table 7 shows only moderate correlation (0.26)

Real image reference quality concerns: 12k→3k images filtered using CLIPScore (the criticized metric); web-scraped images are inherently biased and may not represent valid variations; no quality analysis by country
Incomplete cross-model evaluation: proprietary models limited to 1 image each due to costs, preventing diversity evaluation; diversity metrics only for 3 public models limits generalizability

Statistical rigor issues: no confidence intervals or significance testing; threshold τ calibrated at only 3 percentiles with minimal sensitivity analysis; human-human agreement moderate (0.42, with unexplained GN=0.30 vs GS=0.46)

Methodological design choices lack justification: why these 5 descriptor dimensions? Equal weighting in Faithfulness equation (Eq. 5) is unprincipled; alignment alone achieves 0.33 vs 0.38 composite (modest improvement)
Potential metric design flaw: Hallucination metric may penalize models generating valid but uncommon cultural variations; descriptor-based approach may miss holistic cultural understanding
Limited human evaluation coverage: only 7/16 countries and 3/6 models evaluated with humans; diversity metrics not validated; raises generalizability questions for remaining 9 countries
Crude regional classification: Global North/South binary loses nuance; China (classified South) outperforms some North countries but this outlier not adequately analyzed
Incomplete baseline comparison: CuRe (concurrent work) only briefly discussed; unclear how much improvement derives from novel metrics vs. descriptors vs. proposer-refiner

strengths: Addresses important underexplored problem: cultural faithfulness evaluation through social activities, moving beyond object-centric benchmarks
Comprehensive benchmark contribution: CULTIVate with 19,000+ images, 576 activities, 16 countries spanning Global North/South
Well-designed multi-dimensional evaluation framework: Alignment, Hallucination, Exaggeration, Diversity metrics are complementary and interpretable
Strong empirical results: FAITH achieves 27% higher correlation with human judgment (0.47) vs. MLLM baselines (0.20); demonstrates ITA metrics correlate poorly with human judgment
Thorough validation: 798 human annotations across 11 countries with detailed ablations (Tables 3-5) justify all metric components
Important finding: systematic 4-8% performance gap between Global North and Global South across all models, revealing systematic bias
Interpretable feedback: descriptor-level output enables diagnosis of specific failures and enables image editing applications
Strong reproducibility: extensive implementation details, prompts in appendix, descriptor validation (90% precision)
weaknesses: Fundamental limitation: Reference descriptors generated by LLMs which encode Western biases; using LLM-generated descriptors to evaluate T2I models creates potential circular bias that is acknowledged but not deeply addressed

Moderate inter-rater agreement (Krippendorff's Alpha 0.15-0.62, mean 0.33) reveals high subjectivity in cultural evaluation; human-human agreement (0.55) only marginally better than FAITH (0.47), limiting room for improvement
Contradictory use of ITA metrics: Paper criticizes ITA metrics' unreliability for cultural evaluation but uses VQAScore-based ITA in EXAG metric definition (Eq. 4), undermining this criticism

Threshold calibration lacks theoretical justification: τ selected at 75th percentile based on real images that themselves have biases; different thresholds needed for different MLLMs (0.52 vs 0.67) suggests fragility

Descriptor precision/recall incompletely validated: 90% precision reported but recall estimated indirectly through ratings (4.5/5) and missing descriptor counts (26/378) rather than direct measurement

Limited evaluation scope: Only 11 of 16 countries in human evaluation; 1-2 activities per category; 398 forms with 796 annotations is relatively small; proprietary T2I models evaluated with only 1 image each
Modest inter-rater agreement combined with direct real image filtering via CLIPScore (which paper critiques) creates methodological circularity in calibration
FAITH metric uses simple arithmetic mean of ALIGN, HAL, EXAG without justified weighting or ablation on aggregation method
Missing error analysis: Limited investigation of when/why FAITH diverges from human judgment; no analysis of why Global North models systematically outperform Global South
Limited generalization: Fixed prompt template ('A photorealistic photo...'); unclear if findings generalize to other prompt styles; only 6 T2I models tested
Descriptor-guided editing demonstration is preliminary (Fig. 8) without quantitative evaluation or analysis of scaling and prompt sensitivity

strengths: Addresses important understudied problem: evaluating cultural faithfulness in T2I models through social activities rather than static artifacts
Comprehensive benchmark (CULTIVate) with 576 activities across 16 countries, 19,000+ images, and multi-country human evaluation
Convincingly demonstrates limitations of existing ITA metrics (CLIPScore, ImageReward correlation <0.15 with human judgment)
Identifies Global North/South performance disparity (4-8% gap) across all T2I models
Interpretable diagnostic feedback (top-k descriptor lists) enables targeted error analysis beyond opaque scoring
Systematic benchmark construction using knowledge bases; documented quality controls in human evaluation
Proposer-refiner approach for generating diverse reference descriptors improves over single-stage generation
weaknesses: Fundamental circularity: uses biased LLM-generated descriptors to evaluate potentially biased T2I models; cannot decompose model bias from evaluation apparatus bias; no validation against expert-curated ground truth descriptors

Limited metric novelty: ALIGN/HAL are threshold-based set operations with weak theoretical justification; FAITH is simple arithmetic mean without principled weighting or ablation; EXAG uses LLM-generated stereotypes (adding bias layer)
Weak inter-rater agreement on human gold standard (Krippendorff's α=0.15-0.62, some as low as 0.15), undermining reliability of reference judgments across countries

Metric design choices poorly justified: τ calibrated to arbitrary Q3 percentile (no sensitivity analysis despite Table 5 showing variation); why arithmetic mean vs learned weights; asymmetric ALIGN/HAL formulations unexplained
Unbalanced experimental design: 10 images per prompt (public models) vs 1 image (proprietary models); real image filtering via criticized CLIPScore; limits comparative validity
Empirical gains modest: FAITH correlation=0.47 (InternVL3) vs human-human=0.58 ceiling (0.11 gap); per-model instability (Table 6: ρ ranges -0.14 to 0.51 for same MLLM)

Finding novelty limited: ITA metric failures expected from known VLM limitations; alignment insufficiency obvious; Global North bias unsurprising; China performance unexplored despite contradicting GS/GN hypothesis

Reproducibility concerns: LLM versions mutable; real images via Google Search volatile; proprietary models non-reproducible; only 2 MLLM backbones tested; no sensitivity analysis to architectural choices
Preliminary descriptor-guided editing: only 4 examples (Figure 8), no user study validation, unclear practical adoption; not demonstrated at scale

Incomplete analysis: why China (Global South) outperforms other GS countries? Limited discussion of solutions; ethical concerns (non-English prompts, misuse potential) underexplored; conflates deviation from typical images with cultural faithfulness

strengths: Novel and important problem focusing on social activities for cultural evaluation, capturing compositional and contextual aspects better than object-centric approaches
Substantial benchmark (CULTIVate) with 576 activities, 16 countries, 19,000+ images, 6 T2I models, and comprehensive human evaluation with 796 annotations
Clever Proposer-Refiner methodology for generating robust reference descriptors without relying on inherent biases of VLM embeddings (90% precision on descriptors)
Strong empirical evidence that existing ITA metrics are ineffective (correlations < 0.15) while proposed FAITH metric achieves 27% higher correlation with human judgment (0.47 vs 0.13)
Multi-dimensional decomposition (Alignment, Hallucination, Exaggeration) provides interpretable diagnostic feedback enabling targeted image editing and model improvement
Clear quantification of systematic Global North bias (4-8% advantage) across all evaluated T2I models, with actionable analysis of model performance by country and activity
Excellent reproducibility through detailed implementation details, threshold calibration procedures, and complete prompt specifications in appendix
Rigorous ablation studies (Proposer-Refiner, threshold τ) and comprehensive per-model/per-country/per-dimension analyses revealing systematic patterns
weaknesses: Ground truth validity concerns: LLM-generated reference descriptors may encode Western-centric biases; 90% precision leaves 10% error; Proposer-Refiner mitigation is helpful but partial. Unclear if framework systematically favors Global North.
Moderate inter-rater agreement (α: 0.15–0.62, mean 0.50) raises reliability concerns about human labels; counterintuitively, lower agreement for Global North despite models performing better there

EXAG metric design uses ITA-based approach (VQAScore) despite critiquing ITA metrics, creating methodological circularity; trade-off between interpretability and performance (MLLM-based) insufficiently justified
Web-scraped reference images used for EXAG calibration may themselves contain stereotypes/biases, limiting the validity of using them as baseline for measuring exaggeration
Descriptor recall measured only indirectly (coverage rating 4.5/5; 26/378 annotators reported missing descriptors); systematic measurement of completeness lacking
Limited analysis of DDIV and SDIV metrics introduced in the framework; unclear how important descriptor diversity is for evaluating cultural faithfulness

All evaluations use fixed template ('A photorealistic photo of {activity} in {country}'); unknown whether findings generalize to diverse prompting strategies, creative descriptions, or different prompt structures
Human evaluation smaller than full benchmark (11 vs. 16 countries, 1-2 activities per category); insufficient coverage for validating framework across all regions
Limited failure analysis: Figure 3b identifies hard activities but provides minimal explanation of why (training data representation vs. genuine difficulty)
Potential MLLM bias not thoroughly explored: descriptor extraction relies on InternVL3/Qwen2.5-VL which may themselves have cultural biases, introducing systematic errors for non-Western contexts
Benchmark coverage still limited for some regions (Central Asia, Oceania, parts of Southeast Asia underrepresented relative to Global North)
Scalability concerns: approach requires substantial LLM/MLLM computation for each new model; computational cost of descriptor generation not discussed
